newsitem.title: UK: Xmas brings retailers cheer, but no 80s-style boom.
newsitem.headline: Xmas brings retailers cheer, but no 80s-style boom.

text.p: Christmas cheer could come late this year for British retailers despite predictions for a 1980s-style splurge this December.
Analysts and industry watchers say the pace of sales seems to have slowed in the past few weeks and a few stores already have "sale" slapped across window displays.
Sales in November were very strong still according to official figures published on Wednesday but since then demand seems to have cooled.
"I have to say Christmas sales over the last two weeks have been a bit disappointing," said Peter Williams, finance director at Selfridges, one of London's top department stores.

Industry sources said it was wrong to say demand was going off the boil as Christmas sales would show a healthy increase over 1995, but hopes for a return to the boom-time 1980s now looked over optimistic.
"The level of business is not meeting these expectations," said one industry executive.
Rises in mortgage rates this month, worries about job security and uncertainty ahead of next year's election may have made people more nervous about spending lavishly.
But analysts said it was traditional for retailers to panic in the run up to Christmas.

"It's not a return to the free spending 1980s, but it will be the best Christmas since 1988," said John Richards, retail analyst at NatWest Markets. He predicted five to six percent growth in sales volumes year on year.
Nervousness about retailer performance put fashion chain Next Plc's shares in a spin on Tuesday. The stock sank to a five-week low on worries sales might be flagging.
But chief executive David Jones told Reuters tills were ringing nicely and there was no intention of cutting prices.
Out-of-town shopping centres have been doing a roaring trade at the expense of traditional shopping streets.

Lakeside, a mall just east of London, has had record trading for the past four to six weeks. "It's been tremendous," said spokesman Chris Fear. He said 700,000 shoppers visited last week, up 12 percent on last year.

The hot sellers this year seem to be sportswear -- especially football kits -- household and home furnishings, computers and electricals. But clothing and footwear seem to have been struggling in recent weeks, analysts said.
On Tuesday textile firm Coast Viyella Plc said home furnishings had picked up, but results in UK clothing had been mixed and margins were tight.
This could be bad news for clothing retailers who were expecting this year's strong retail sales trend to deliver a really sparkling Christmas.
"Those who stocked up on the basis that it would be fantastic will be sweating," said one retail analyst.
But in general stores have learnt to be more cautious on stocks and are less likely to be caught out than in previous years, said Hugh Clark, trading policy director at the British Retail Consortium
"Things are about in line," he said, "They are just a little quieter than in the previous few months."
But margins could be squeezed, despite worries that inflation could be gathering steam in the wider economy. The retail price index has risen, but within that retail goods have not gone up.
"There's no reason to see a major improvement in margin," said Clark.
